cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the scale in your hands stays even.
cells.act: let the old form go so the next one can come
cells.ask: Let a finished thing end plainly — a habit, a plan, a version of someone you carry — and clear the room it leaves. Then keep tending what's still alive.
cells.core:
What you tend gets the size and room it needs. You can feel what a growing thing is owed without running the numbers, and what you give comes back without a ledger sitting between you. That calm eye is also what spots the endings: the way you two talk, a plan that had its day, a role you keep playing past its point.

When something has finished, you can let it close and clear the space it leaves, and nothing about that is harsh. It's the same fairness turned toward what's next. What you let end makes room under your hands, and what's still growing gets the light. Let one finished thing close, and you'll see how little was actually lost.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what grows, and you can tell when it's done.
cells.verb: to weigh what is fair and set it right
cells.place: where you tend what is still growing

cells.tense: You are braced already for the day your care comes back owed to you.
cells.act: bear the next hour of it without deciding anything
cells.ask: Carry one growing thing without ruling on what you're owed back. No count, no verdict — let it sit at whatever size it is.
cells.core:
The scale tips into counting. Who gave what, who owes, what you're owed for your work — you get out front of what's growing and add up what it hasn't produced yet. The thing stays small because it's been weighed before it could ripen, and the people you tend feel the tally even when you don't say it.

Spend an hour with the same thing and don't measure it. Don't decide, don't correct the count — just hold it at the size it actually is. That's the harder strength, the kind that contains rather than crushes. An hour of that, once, and you'll feel where your grip had slipped. A hand that stops moving the scale lets it go quiet.

cells.verb: to weigh what is fair and set it right

cells.tense: You still stand at the door where you last asked for what you were owed.
cells.act: do the plain version first, before the plans
cells.ask: Do the plain version of something today, alone — the unglamorous part, with no plan built around it. Do it again tomorrow the same way.
cells.core:
In one area you're not claiming what you're owed. What you give keeps going out and little comes back, and asking has come to feel like a risk, so you stopped. The scale still sits in you. It just doesn't get used on your own behalf.

Pushing harder won't settle anything. Small, repeated, and yours alone is what works: the plain version of a practice, done again and again, no audience, no outcome riding on it. Doing that unglamorous piece today is the whole ask. This isn't about the person across from you — it's what's fair coming back into your own hands, kept lit from inside, tended by you the way you tend everything else.

cells.tense: The pen is down, and you are still writing in a room you don't know you're in.
cells.act: write the first thing you knew about it, before the reasons
cells.ask: About one situation you're tending, put the first impression on paper before any argument for it. Leave the arguments off the page.
cells.core:
The fairness is running below your own waterline. You don't experience yourself as weighing anything — unless someone holds up a mirror — and there's a tally of what people owe you that's been kept below the surface, steering where your attention goes.

The way out isn't a better accounting. It's earlier than that. About whatever you're tending, something arrived before the reasons and the verdicts, before you built the case. Put that first impression on paper, not the argument for it. What's fair doesn't need to be argued into place; you tend better from the thing you saw first, and looking at it plainly costs no trust.
